question: Which element of the boron family has a high boiling point, making it ideal for recording temperatures that would vaporise a thermometer?
solution:
The Correct answer is __**Gallium**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **​Gallium (Ga)** is a member of the boron family, positioned in **Group 13 of the Periodic Table**, with an **atomic number of 31 **and a relative **atomic mass of 69.723**.
 
• Gallium possesses a notably high boiling point of around** 2200°C **(3992°F), rendering it suitable for applications requiring the measurement of extreme temperatures that would vaporize conventional thermometers.
 
• Gallium finds various applications:
 
 
• **Specialized Thermometers: **Gallium is utilized in specialized thermometers engineered for high temperatures. These gallium thermometers provide a safe and accurate alternative to traditional mercury thermometers, which pose hazards due to mercury toxicity.
 
• **Semiconductor Production:** Gallium is a crucial constituent in semiconductor manufacturing. Gallium arsenide (GaAs) is employed to fabricate high-frequency electronic devices like microwave transistors and light-emitting diodes (LEDs).
 
• **Alloying Agent: **Gallium is alloyed with other metals to produce materials with specific properties. For instance, gallium-indium-tin alloys are utilized in liquid metal cooling systems for electronics, offering efficient heat transfer capabilities.
 
• **Nuclear Medicine:** Gallium-67, a radioactive isotope of gallium, plays a vital role in nuclear medicine for diagnostic imaging purposes. It is utilized to detect and diagnose certain diseases, aiding in medical diagnostics and treatment planning.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Thallium **belongs to the boron family, specifically Group 13, in the periodic table, with an atomic number of 81. Due to its relatively low boiling point, thallium is not suitable for measuring high temperatures that would cause a thermometer to vaporize.
 
• **Aluminium** is another member of the boron family, with an atomic number of 13. While aluminium has a moderate boiling point, it is not exceptionally high, making it unsuitable for recording extremely high temperatures.
 
• **Indium** is also part of the boron family, with an atomic number of 49. Compared to gallium, indium has a lower boiling point, rendering it less suitable for applications requiring the measurement of high temperatures.
